newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Taleban say warplane shot down after bombing.
newsitem.headline: Taleban say warplane shot down after bombing.

text.p: The Taleban militia ruling Kabul said on Saturday a warplane which bombed the Afghan capital and killed three children was shot down as it flew back north.

The official radio, renamed Radio Sharia after Islam's stern law which the Taleban want to impose on Afghanistan, said the plane was brought down by "special guided missiles" after a bombing run over Kabul on Thursday.
It said the pilot was killed when his plane was brought down over the Kohdaman mountains north of Kabul after he "bombed Kabul city's residential areas".
There was no independent confirmation of what would be the first known shooting down of a warplane since the Taleban took Kabul on September 27.
A northern alliance between Uzbek leader Abdul Rashid Dostum and the ousted government's military chief Ahmad Shah Masood has been battling towards Kabul for the past two weeks.

Dostum, who has a small air force, has conducted several air raids on Kabul over the past week, most of them aimed at the airport on the northeastern edge of the city which is used for both civilian and military traffic.
Although one of the first bombs landed at night in a city centre park, there had been no civilian casualties in the raids until Thursday.
But then one plane dropped two 250 kg (550 lb) bombs on a northwestern residential area, destroying two houses, killing three children were killed and wounding seven people, some seriously.
Local people said the attack was probably aimed at a nearby military base.
The other raids on the airport have failed to damage it and it remains open to traffic.

Radio Sharia did not identify the kind of missile it said brought down Dostum's plane, but the Taleban defenders of Kabul have twice fired surface-to-air missiles at the raiders which experts said were probably Stingers.
The United States supplied the heat-seeking missiles to Moslem mujahideen guerrillas fighting a Soviet-backed communist government in the 1980s.
The mujahideen finally took Kabul in 1992 and were widely believed to still have some Stingers in their arsenals.
The Taleban, born in religious schools in refugee camps in Pakistan two years ago, have been joined by many mujahideen commanders as they swept to control of three-quarters of Afghanistan.
They drove Masood back to his Panjsher Valley stronghold after taking Kabul, but he made an alliance with Dostum and counter-attacked, driving the Taleban back towards Kabul.

The fighting, however, has been deadlocked in a range of hills across the Shamali Valley 25 to 30 km (15 to 19 miles) north of the capital despite a series of attempts by the alliance to break through Taleban lines.
Thursday's bombing raids on Kabul were launched shortly after the alliance launched its latest attempt to break through the hills.
The attempt failed and the front lines have not changed significantly.
